title: UT Level 2 Practice Questions: 30 Questions with Answers
metaDescription: 30 original UT Level II practice questions with answers and explanations: physics, calibration, angle-beam scanning, interpretation, codes and limits.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Level II Practice Questions
intro: These 30 multiple-choice questions are original study questions written by Atlantis NDT for ultrasonic technicians preparing for a Level II examination. They are not ASNT exam questions. They cover the work a Level II is expected to do: set up and calibrate the equipment, carry out straight-beam and angle-beam examinations, interpret and evaluate indications against a procedure, and report the results.

Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition), the employer certifies Level II technicians after general, specific and practical examinations set out in its written practice. ASNT also runs central ASNT NDT Level II examinations (general and method exams); where those are used, the employer still carries out the visual acuity, practical and job-specific examinations. Use this set to find weak areas before either route.

Atlantis NDT runs NDT training year-round, with theory online and hands-on practice on its Practical NDT simulator or in person at the client's own facility. Simulator practice supports training; it does not replace the practical examination or the experience hours the employer's written practice requires.
howToUse: Answer each question before opening the explanation, and write down your choice.
Work the calculations on paper with units; most errors come from mixing millimeters, meters and microseconds.
Note the topics where you miss more than one question and study those first.
Re-test after a few days of study and compare your results by topic, not just overall.

questions.q: What is the approximate wavelength of a 5 MHz longitudinal wave in steel (velocity 5,900 m/s)?
questions.explanation: λ = v/f = 5,900 m/s ÷ 5,000,000 Hz = 0.00118 m, or about 1.18 mm. 2.36 mm would be the wavelength at 2.5 MHz.

questions.q: Using N = D²·f/(4v), what is the approximate near-field length of a 10 mm diameter, 5 MHz straight-beam probe in steel (longitudinal velocity 5,900 m/s)?
questions.explanation: N = (10 mm)² × 5,000,000 Hz ÷ (4 × 5,900,000 mm/s) = 5×10⁸ ÷ 2.36×10⁷ ≈ 21.2 mm. Doubling the diameter would quadruple N, not double it.

questions.q: What is the main reason a liquid or gel couplant is used between a contact transducer and a steel part?
options: It displaces air, whose very low acoustic impedance would reflect almost all the sound
It raises the frequency of the transmitted pulse so that smaller flaws can be resolved
It converts the longitudinal wave into a shear wave as the sound enters the steel
It shortens the near field of the transducer
questions.explanation: Acoustic impedance (density × velocity) of air is several orders of magnitude lower than that of steel, so an air gap gives almost total reflection. Couplant displaces the air; it does not change the frequency or the wave mode.

questions.q: An acrylic wedge (longitudinal velocity 2,730 m/s) is to produce a 45° refracted shear wave in steel (shear velocity 3,230 m/s). What incident angle is required?
questions.explanation: Snell's law: sin θi = (2,730 ÷ 3,230) × sin 45° = 0.845 × 0.707 ≈ 0.598, so θi ≈ 36.7°. 57.7° is the second critical angle for this wedge and steel combination.

questions.q: For an acrylic wedge on steel, what happens when the incident angle exceeds the second critical angle?
options: Only a refracted longitudinal wave exists in the steel
Both longitudinal and shear waves are refracted into the steel
Neither a longitudinal nor a shear bulk wave is refracted into the steel
The refracted shear wave travels at exactly 45°
questions.explanation: Beyond the first critical angle the refracted longitudinal wave is lost; beyond the second critical angle the refracted shear wave is lost too (near the second critical angle a surface wave is generated). Shear-wave probes therefore use incident angles between the two critical angles.

questions.q: On an IIW-type calibration block (ISO 2400 block No. 1), what is the 100 mm radius mainly used for with an angle-beam probe?
options: Checking the near-surface resolution of a straight-beam probe
Measuring the refracted angle of the beam in steel
Measuring the beam spread and focal distance of a dual-element probe
Locating the probe index point and calibrating the sound-path range
questions.explanation: Maximizing the echo from the 100 mm radius places the probe index point at the center of the arc, and the radius echo and its repeat set the time base in sound path. The refracted angle is checked separately, using the holes and angle scales on the block.

questions.q: Compared with a lightly damped transducer of the same frequency, what does a heavily damped (broadband) transducer generally give?
options: Better depth resolution but lower sensitivity
Poorer depth resolution but higher sensitivity
A longer pulse containing more cycles
A narrower bandwidth around the center frequency
questions.explanation: Heavy backing damping shortens the pulse to fewer cycles, which broadens the bandwidth and improves the separation of closely spaced reflectors in depth, at the cost of some sensitivity.

questions.q: What does a screen height (vertical) linearity check confirm?
options: That the time base is accurate across the full screen width
That two echoes keep their amplitude ratio as the gain is changed
That the probe frequency matches its marked value
That the pulse repetition rate is low enough to avoid ghost echoes
questions.explanation: Screen height linearity is checked by setting two echoes at a known amplitude ratio (commonly 2:1) and confirming the ratio holds as the gain is varied, so displayed amplitude is proportional to the received signal. Time-base accuracy is horizontal linearity.
questions.ref: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4 (instrument linearity checks)

questions.q: How is a distance-amplitude correction (DAC) curve normally constructed for angle-beam weld examination?
options: By plotting the back-wall echo heights from a set of plates of different thickness
By plotting the noise level at several gain settings across the screen
By plotting peak echoes from same-size reference reflectors at several sound paths
By plotting echoes from natural flaws in a production weld of the same material
questions.explanation: A DAC joins the maximized responses from same-size reference reflectors, such as side-drilled holes, at increasing sound paths in a block of material similar to the part. It shows how the response from a given reflector falls with distance in that material, and indications are judged against it.
questions.ref: General UT practice; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4

questions.q: An echo peaks at 20% full screen height (FSH). Approximately how much gain must be added to bring it to 80% FSH on a linear display?
options: 6 dB
12 dB
18 dB
24 dB
questions.explanation: The amplitude ratio is 80 ÷ 20 = 4, and 20·log₁₀(4) ≈ 12 dB. Each 6 dB doubles the amplitude: 20% to 40% to 80%.

questions.q: Why do many UT procedures require the reject (suppression) control to be off during calibration and evaluation?
options: It increases the pulse repetition frequency, which can cause ghost echoes
It changes the refracted angle of the probe in the test material
It reduces the near-field length of the transducer
It can hide low-level signals and make the amplitude display non-linear
questions.explanation: Reject suppresses everything below a threshold and, on many instruments, makes the amplitude response non-linear, so low-level flaw echoes can be hidden and comparisons with a DAC become unreliable.

questions.q: What is the full skip distance for a 60° shear-wave probe on a 20 mm thick plate?
questions.explanation: Full skip = 2 × T × tan θ = 2 × 20 × tan 60° = 40 × 1.732 ≈ 69.3 mm. 34.6 mm is the half skip.

questions.q: A 45° probe on a 25 mm plate gives an echo at a sound path of 50 mm. What is the depth of the reflector below the scanning surface?
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = 50 × cos 45° ≈ 35.4 mm, which exceeds the thickness, so the reflector is on the second leg after a bounce off the back wall. True depth = 2T − 35.4 = 50 − 35.4 ≈ 14.6 mm. The surface distance is 50 × sin 45° ≈ 35.4 mm.

questions.q: To detect transverse cracks in a butt weld, in which direction should the angle beam be directed?
options: Perpendicular to the weld axis from both sides
Essentially parallel to the weld axis, on the weld or alongside it
Straight down at 0° through the weld cap only
Toward the heat-affected zone using a surface-wave probe only
questions.explanation: A transverse crack lies across the weld, so the beam must travel roughly along the weld axis to strike its face. Beams directed perpendicular to the weld axis are used for longitudinal flaws.
questions.ref: General UT practice; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4

questions.q: Why do UT procedures require each scan pass to overlap the previous pass?
options: To reduce couplant consumption
To allow the time base to be checked and recalibrated during scanning
To increase the effective refracted angle at the weld fusion faces
To avoid gaps in coverage, as the beam is less sensitive at its edges
questions.explanation: The beam is not uniformly sensitive across its width, so passes are indexed with a specified overlap of the transducer dimension to avoid unexamined strips between passes.

questions.q: Why is manual scanning usually performed at a gain higher than the reference level, with evaluation then carried out at reference sensitivity?
options: To make the near field shorter
Because the reference level is used only for thickness measurement, not flaw detection
So that weak or poorly oriented reflectors are less likely to be missed
To calibrate the time base more accurately on the component
questions.explanation: Extra scanning gain helps detect weak or poorly oriented reflectors during the search. Once an indication is found, its amplitude is evaluated at the reference sensitivity the acceptance criteria are based on.
questions.ref: General UT practice; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4

questions.q: What is a transfer correction (transfer loss measurement) used to compensate for?
options: Differences in surface condition, coupling and attenuation between block and part
Drift in the instrument's time base during a long shift
The wedge delay of a dual-element probe
The difference between longitudinal and shear velocities in the component material
questions.explanation: Comparing the same type of reference signal on the block and on the part shows how much extra loss the part introduces. The gain is adjusted by that amount so the DAC remains valid on the component.

questions.q: During straight-beam testing of a 30 mm steel plate, the back-wall echo disappears over an area and a strong echo appears at about 15 mm depth with its own repeats. What is the most likely cause?
options: Loss of coupling under the probe
A transverse crack open to the scanning surface
Scattered fine porosity through the thickness
A lamination lying parallel to the surface
questions.explanation: A planar reflector parallel to the surface blocks the sound from reaching the back wall and gives a strong echo with multiple repeats. Loss of coupling would remove all echoes, including the mid-wall one.

questions.q: Which angle-beam echo behavior is most typical of a planar crack?
options: An echo that looks the same, and has similar amplitude, from both sides of the weld and from every direction
An echo at a fixed position on the time base that does not move when the probe is moved
Amplitude that varies strongly with beam direction, with a ragged, multi-peaked echo
A cluster of many small, low-amplitude echoes that appear and disappear independently
questions.explanation: A crack is planar and often faceted, so its response is strongly directional with a ragged echo dynamic. A rounded reflector responds similarly from all directions, a cluster of small echoes suggests porosity, and an echo that never moves comes from the probe or wedge, not the part.

questions.q: What is the most reliable way to decide whether an echo from the weld root area is a geometric indication from the root bead rather than a flaw?
options: Raise the gain until the echo saturates, then judge it by its width on the screen
Plot its position on the measured weld profile and confirm it from the opposite side
Accept it as geometric if its peak stays below 100% of full screen height
Change to a higher-frequency probe and treat it as geometric if the echo fades
questions.explanation: Geometric echoes are identified by plotting. A reflector that plots on the root bead or counterbore position, and behaves consistently from the opposite side, is geometric. Amplitude or a change of frequency cannot prove where an echo comes from.

questions.q: In the 6 dB drop method for sizing a reflector that is larger than the beam, the reflector edge is taken where the echo amplitude does what?
options: Falls to half of its maximum value
Falls to 10% FSH
Falls by 20 dB from its maximum
Rises above the DAC curve
questions.explanation: A 6 dB drop halves the amplitude, which corresponds to the beam axis being on the reflector edge. The method is only valid for reflectors larger than the beam; for smaller reflectors it measures the beam width rather than the flaw.

questions.q: Why is echo amplitude alone an unreliable measure of the size of a planar flaw?
options: Because amplitude does not change with distance from the probe
Because amplitude also depends on orientation, roughness and position in the beam
Because larger flaws always give smaller echoes
Because echo amplitude can only be measured accurately with a dual-element contact probe
questions.explanation: A large crack tilted away from the beam, or with a rough face, can give a lower echo than a small, well-oriented reflector. This is why length is sized by probe movement and height is often sized by tip-diffraction techniques rather than by amplitude.

questions.q: During a periodic calibration check, the reference sensitivity is found to have dropped by more than the procedure allows. What is normally required?
options: Increase the gain by the amount lost and carry on scanning from the current position
Record the change in the report and take no further action
Average the old and new sensitivities for all indications
Correct the calibration and re-examine everything done since the last valid check
questions.explanation: If sensitivity fell beyond the tolerance, work done since the last good check may have missed indications, so the calibration is corrected and that work is repeated. ASME Section V Article 4 contains this type of requirement; the procedure sets the tolerance.
questions.ref: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4 (calibration confirmation)

questions.q: Why do procedures require the calibration block to be close in temperature to the component being examined?
options: Because velocity and attenuation, especially in the wedge, change with temperature
Because the block expands enough to change its nominal dimensions and hole positions significantly
Because couplant only works at room temperature, whatever its type
Because the probe frequency doubles when the temperature rises by a few degrees
questions.explanation: Wedge velocity is quite temperature-sensitive, so a temperature difference shifts the refracted angle, the timing and the attenuation. ASME Section V Article 4 limits the block-to-component temperature difference for this reason.
questions.ref: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4 (calibration block temperature)

questions.q: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, which task is normally reserved for a Level III rather than a Level II?
options: Setting up and calibrating the equipment
Interpreting and evaluating results against the applicable code
Approving NDT procedures and establishing techniques
Organizing and reporting examination results
questions.explanation: SNT-TC-1A describes Level II personnel as able to set up and calibrate equipment, interpret and evaluate results against codes, and organize and report results. Developing, qualifying and approving procedures and establishing techniques are Level III responsibilities.

questions.q: Which set of information should a UT report contain so that the examination can be repeated?
options: The accept or reject decision, the date and the technician's signature
Equipment, search units, couplant, calibration block, reference level, procedure and coverage
The part number, the drawing revision and the technician's signature
Screen images of every rejected indication, with the decision for each
questions.explanation: Another qualified technician must be able to reproduce the set-up and coverage from the report. The decision, signature and images are needed too, but on their own they do not allow the examination to be repeated.
questions.ref: General NDT reporting practice; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4

questions.q: For an ASME Section V Article 4 angle-beam examination of a plate (non-piping) weld, which reference reflectors in the basic calibration block are used to build the DAC?
options: Side-drilled holes
Flat-bottom holes drilled from the back face
Spherical voids
Natural cracks from a previous weld
questions.explanation: The non-piping basic calibration block in Article 4 uses side-drilled holes at known depths. Piping calibration blocks use notches, and flat-bottom holes are typical of straight-beam reference blocks.
questions.ref: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4 (calibration blocks)

questions.q: An austenitic stainless steel weld gives high background noise and poor penetration with a 5 MHz shear-wave probe. Which change is most likely to improve the examination?
options: Increase the frequency to 10 MHz to obtain a sharper and better-resolved beam
Use a lower frequency, and consider refracted longitudinal-wave dual probes
Increase the pulse repetition frequency to average out the noise
Use a smaller crystal at the same frequency and the same shear-wave angle
questions.explanation: Coarse, columnar austenitic grains scatter and attenuate sound, more so at higher frequencies and for shear waves. Lower frequency and refracted longitudinal waves reduce scatter and beam skewing.
questions.ref: General UT principle (attenuation in coarse-grained materials)

questions.q: With a single-element contact straight-beam probe, why are reflectors very close to the scanning surface hard to detect?
options: The beam diverges too quickly in the first few millimeters below the probe
Shear waves are generated near the surface and swamp the longitudinal echoes
The back-wall echo arrives first
The initial pulse and ring-down mask echoes from the first few millimeters
questions.explanation: While the transducer is still ringing after excitation it cannot display separate echoes, so the first few millimeters below the surface form a dead zone. Dual-element or delay-line probes move the interface signal away from the near-surface region and reduce this problem.

questions.q: Which flaw is most likely to be missed by a straight-beam (0°) examination from the plate surface?
options: A lamination in the parent plate lying parallel to the surface
A slag inclusion lying flat and parallel to the plate surface
A large, rounded gas pore near the middle of the plate thickness
A vertical planar flaw, such as sidewall lack of fusion in a square-edge joint
questions.explanation: A 0° beam travels parallel to a vertical planar flaw, so almost no energy is reflected back to the probe. Angle beams are used to strike such flaws at a favorable angle.
